subsections.subsection_title: 36. DIFFERENTIAL WHEN THE HEAD IS NOT DESCENDING

blocks.text: If there is failure of descent, think:

content_groups.group_title: Q1. What are the indications for operative vaginal delivery?

blocks.text: Fetal compromise requiring expedited birth, maternal indications such as exhaustion or inability to push effectively, and prolonged or arrested second stage where vaginal delivery remains appropriate.

Full cervical dilatation, ruptured membranes, engaged fetal head, known fetal position, appropriate station, adequate pelvis, empty bladder, appropriate analgesia, informed consent where possible, a skilled operator and facilities for emergency Caesarean delivery if required.

content_groups.group_title: Q3. What is the most important thing before applying forceps?

blocks.text: Confirm the fetal head's position and station and ensure that all prerequisites for safe operative vaginal delivery are fulfilled.

content_groups.group_title: Q4. What are the maternal complications?

blocks.text: Perineal and vaginal trauma, severe perineal tears, postpartum haemorrhage, haematoma, pain and longer-term pelvic-floor, urinary or bowel dysfunction.

content_groups.group_title: Q5. What are the complications of vacuum?

blocks.text: Scalp trauma, chignon, cephalohaematoma, jaundice and, rarely, serious bleeding such as subgaleal or intracranial haemorrhage.

content_groups.group_title: Q6. What are the complications of forceps?

blocks.text: Maternal perineal trauma, postpartum haemorrhage and neonatal facial bruising, facial nerve injury and, rarely, more serious trauma.

content_groups.group_title: Q7. What would you do if the vacuum repeatedly pops off?

blocks.text: Stop and reassess the situation rather than repeatedly attempting traction. Confirm position, application and descent, reassess whether operative vaginal delivery remains appropriate and consider an alternative method or Caesarean delivery.

content_groups.group_title: Q8. What if there is no descent with traction?

blocks.text: Stop, reassess fetal position, station, application and the possibility of disproportion or obstruction. I would seek senior assistance and avoid repeated unsuccessful attempts.

content_groups.group_title: Q9. When would you choose Caesarean section instead?

blocks.text: When vaginal delivery is not imminent or cannot safely be achieved, when prerequisites for instrumental delivery are not fulfilled, when the fetal head is too high or the position is unknown, or when an instrumental attempt has failed.
A 30-year-old primigravida at 40+2 weeks has been pushing for an extended period.
The fetal head is low in the pelvis.

“I would first assess the maternal and fetal condition and confirm the fetal head position and station. If the cervix is fully dilated, membranes are ruptured, the head is appropriately low, the position is known and there is no contraindication, I would consider an operative vaginal delivery if a rapid vaginal birth is appropriate. I would discuss vacuum versus forceps based on the clinical situation and operator expertise. If the prerequisites are not fulfilled or vaginal delivery is unlikely to succeed, I would proceed to emergency Caesarean delivery.”
“You have attempted vacuum delivery but there has been no descent. What do you do?”

“I would stop the procedure and reassess rather than continuing repeated traction. I would reassess the fetal position and station, the cup application, maternal and fetal condition and whether there may be disproportion or obstruction. I would call for senior assistance and determine whether another appropriately performed instrumental attempt is reasonable or whether Caesarean delivery is safer.”

**INDICATION → ASSESS HEAD → CONFIRM PREREQUISITES → CONSENT → CHOOSE INSTRUMENT → PERFORM → REASSESS → KNOW WHEN TO STOP → MANAGE COMPLICATIONS**

“Operative vaginal delivery is used to expedite vaginal birth for appropriate fetal, maternal or labour indications. Before proceeding, I would confirm full cervical dilatation, ruptured membranes, an engaged head, known fetal position and appropriate station, adequate pelvis, an empty bladder, appropriate analgesia, informed consent where possible, skilled personnel and the ability to perform Caesarean delivery if required. I would explain the benefits, alternatives and maternal and neonatal risks. I would select vacuum or forceps based on the clinical circumstances and operator expertise, apply the instrument correctly and use controlled traction with contractions and maternal effort. If there is no descent or the procedure is unsuccessful, I would stop, reassess and proceed to an alternative appropriate mode of delivery rather than persisting with repeated attempts. Following delivery, I would assess both mother and baby for complications and document the procedure fully.”
